paragraphs: Giving a multimodal model access to tools creates another decision: whether a particular question actually needs them. Unnecessary or unsuitable calls can add work and lead the model toward an incorrect answer. AutoTool addresses this decision directly, learning when to use tool assistance and when to rely on text-centric reasoning.

The training framework uses reinforcement learning with two explicit reasoning modes and separate reward functions for each. It encourages exploration of both modes and balances them during training so that the model does not settle prematurely on one approach. Later training allows freer exploration, supporting query-dependent choices rather than a fixed preference for tool use.

The experiments report a 21.8% accuracy gain over the base model on V* and a 44.9% efficiency improvement over existing tool-augmented methods on POPE. These results concern different benchmarks and comparisons. Together, they support treating tool selection as part of the reasoning problem: performance depends on choosing useful assistance as well as knowing how to invoke it.
icml-2026-are-tools-always-beneficial-le.tldr: AutoTool learns when to use tools or text-centric reasoning, improving reported accuracy and efficiency through adaptive selection.

paragraphs: Meta-learning transfers experience from previously learned tasks to new ones, but that experience can become harmful when the new task differs substantially. This paper addresses such negative transfer by organizing transfer around causal task embeddings: compact representations intended to capture similarities in underlying mechanisms rather than incidental correlations.

The method uses these precomputed embeddings to condition task-specific Bayesian priors, which express what the learner expects before observing much target-task data. It explicitly considers limited access to that data. Instead, adaptation can use noisy expert judgments comparing the causal similarity of source and target tasks, making expert feedback part of the transfer process.

The theoretical analysis shows that conditioning on causal embeddings controls prior mismatch and mitigates negative transfer under task shift. Experiments report improvements in controlled simulations and clinical prediction across diseases. In the clinical setting, the embeddings align with underlying mechanisms, and incorporating a medical expert’s judgments improves predictions for unseen diseases. The findings support mechanism-sensitive transfer in the studied settings, including when target examples are scarce.
icml-2026-bayesian-meta-learning-with-ex.tldr: Causal task embeddings and noisy expert feedback help Bayesian meta-learning reduce harmful transfer to unfamiliar tasks.

paragraphs: Multimodal prediction often encounters incomplete examples: one source of information may be absent, collected at a different time, or available for only some cases. PRIMO addresses both prediction with missing modalities and the question of how much those missing inputs could affect a particular prediction. It can train on complete and partial examples together.

PRIMO represents a missing modality through a latent variable learned in relation to the observed input and prediction target. At inference, it samples many possible latent completions. Averaging predictions across these possibilities produces a prediction that accounts for the missing information, while variation between those predictions measures its potential influence for that individual example.

Evaluations cover synthetic XOR data, Audio-Vision MNIST, and MIMIC-III mortality and ICD-9 prediction. Performance is comparable to unimodal baselines when a modality is entirely absent and to multimodal baselines when all are present. The variance-based impact measure adds an interpretation layer: different plausible completions can support different labels, revealing where the unobserved modality matters.
icml-2026-characterizing-the-predictive-.tldr: PRIMO predicts from incomplete multimodal data and measures how much a missing modality could change each prediction.

paragraphs: Tiny targets in infrared video can look like little more than points, giving a detector very little recognizable object information. Background pixels also greatly outnumber target pixels, which can undermine useful representations. CodeMamba changes the emphasis: it combines learning the background’s regular structure with detecting unusual movement across frames.

The framework has two cooperating streams. The implicit stream models background regularity and identifies departures from it. The explicit stream examines motion consistency and unusual patterns across space and time. These views provide complementary evidence about whether a small signal belongs to a target or to dynamic background clutter, rather than relying primarily on target appearance.

A Bayesian fusion module combines the streams according to their estimated uncertainty. It quantifies observation noise to assess how reliable each stream is, allowing their contributions to reflect that reliability. Experiments on IRDST and DAUB report better performance than existing methods and greater sensitivity to point-like targets. The results support combining background modeling with motion evidence for this difficult detection setting.
icml-2026-codemamba-shifting-from-target.tldr: CodeMamba combines background regularity, motion anomalies, and uncertainty-weighted fusion to improve tiny infrared target detection.

paragraphs: Adapting a foundation model to a specific task can be difficult when high-quality labeled examples are scarce. This paper asks whether users working on similar tasks can help one another during adaptation. Its proposed method, Collaborative Low-Rank Adaptation, or CoLoRA, combines shared learning with user-specific customization through efficient adapters.

CoLoRA trains one shared adapter to capture structure common across tasks, alongside personalized adapters that capture what each user’s task requires. This arrangement gives task similarity an explicit role in adaptation. Shared information can support multiple users, while the personalized component preserves a way to represent differences between their prediction problems.

The authors analyze CoLoRA theoretically for heterogeneous linear regression and provide guarantees for recovering the ground truth in that setting. They also evaluate natural language tasks with varying degrees of similarity. Those experiments show significant individual performance improvements when similar tasks are trained together. The findings support collaboration as a response to scarce task data, with task similarity central to the reported benefit.
icml-2026-collaborative-and-efficient-fi.tldr: CoLoRA combines shared and personalized low-rank adapters so similar tasks can benefit from collaborative fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Some learning algorithms update two interacting sets of parameters at different speeds. Establishing that these updates remain bounded and eventually converge becomes more difficult when successive observations are dependent. This paper studies that situation using Markovian noise, a setting relevant to reinforcement learning because observations arrive through an evolving process.

The analysis establishes stability and convergence for two-timescale stochastic approximation under this noise model. It does not require a projection operator to force parameters back into a bounded region, and the noise need not occupy a compact space. The key proof technique controls the fast parameters using the running maximum of the slow parameters, rather than only their current values.

A principal application concerns temporal difference learning with gradient correction and eligibility traces. The paper establishes its first almost sure convergence result for off-policy learning with linear function approximation. This connects the general mathematical argument to a concrete reinforcement learning method, extending convergence analysis to dependent observations without the stated projection or compact-noise requirements.
icml-2026-convergence-of-two-timescale-m.tldr: A new stability argument establishes two-timescale convergence under Markovian noise and yields an off-policy TDC convergence result.

paragraphs: Models with enough parameters to overfit their training examples can amplify bias associated with spurious correlations. The paper analyzes why conventional fairness-constrained empirical risk minimization can fail in this regime. Its central finding is that the fairness constraint can be adjusted to allow bias overcompensation, correcting the effect identified by the analysis.

The work also gives an empirical criterion for strong equalized odds based on representer coefficients. These coefficients describe how training examples contribute to the fitted model. Balancing their group-conditional means corresponds to equal average contributions from sensitive groups, providing a concrete quantity to examine when choosing the amount of overcompensation.

Building on this criterion, the authors derive an estimable search interval that narrows where the required overcompensation level should lie. This turns the analysis into guidance for adjusting the fairness constraint. Although the results are asymptotic, the paper reports that they closely describe the statistical behavior of moderately large models, connecting the theoretical correction to a more practically relevant model scale.
icml-2026-correcting-overparameterizatio.tldr: Allowing calibrated bias overcompensation can correct fairness constraints that fail in the analyzed overparameterized regime.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when an adversary can corrupt some observed rewards. The objective is to learn an optimal policy for an infinite-horizon problem with discounted future rewards. The authors consider asynchronous sampling with time-correlated observations, bringing dependence between samples directly into the robustness analysis.

They develop a robust variant of Q-learning and prove finite-time guarantees that match existing bounds except for an additional term scaling with the fraction of corrupted samples. This separates ordinary learning error from the cost of reward corruption. An information-theoretic lower bound shows that the resulting guarantees are near-optimal, rather than merely establishing that the method tolerates some corruption.

The algorithm does not need to know the underlying reward distribution. The paper presents its result as the first finite-time robustness guarantee for asynchronous Q-learning. Its analysis also develops a refined Azuma-Hoeffding inequality for almost-martingales, a mathematical tool for controlling dependent fluctuations. The authors identify possible applications of that inequality to the analysis of other reinforcement learning algorithms.
icml-2026-corruption-tolerant-asynchrono.tldr: Robust asynchronous Q-learning achieves near-optimal finite-time guarantees with an added error term tied to reward corruption.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation depends on finding documents that genuinely match a question. HypRAG investigates whether the geometry used to represent documents can improve this matching. Its motivation is that language contains hierarchies, from broad topics to specific entities, and that conventional Euclidean embeddings can place semantically distant documents misleadingly close together.

The paper develops two retrievers in hyperbolic space. HyTE-FH uses a fully hyperbolic transformer, while HyTE-H projects pretrained Euclidean embeddings into that space. It also introduces the Outward Einstein Midpoint, a pooling operation designed to combine sequence representations without collapse and with a stated mathematical guarantee of preserving hierarchical structure.

HyTE-FH outperforms equivalent Euclidean baselines on MTEB. On RAGBench, HyTE-H reports gains of up to 29% in context and answer relevance over Euclidean baselines while using substantially smaller models than current leading retrievers. Analysis finds more than 20% radial separation growth from general to specific concepts. This supports the proposed connection between embedding geometry, document specificity, and retrieval relevance.
icml-2026-hyprag-hyperbolic-dense-retrie.tldr: HypRAG uses hyperbolic embeddings and hierarchy-preserving pooling to improve retrieval and answer relevance in reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Proteins function through collections of changing conformations, so a useful generator must produce ensembles consistent with experimental observations. This paper introduces inference-time optimization to address problems in diffusion guidance, including fixed sampling horizons, initialization sensitivity, and physically implausible results. It optimizes latent representations to maximize ensemble likelihood instead of adjusting generated structures afterward.

The framework also introduces sampling schemes for Boltzmann-weighted ensembles. These combine structural priors from AlphaFold3 with force-field priors, sampling from their product while incorporating experimental likelihoods. The approach is designed to remove dependence on diffusion length and initialization bias, while making it straightforward to include additional external constraints.

Reported results improve diversity, physical energy, and agreement with X-ray crystallography and NMR data compared with leading guidance methods. Some ensembles fit observations better than deposited PDB structures. A separate experiment shows that changing MSA embeddings can artificially increase iPTM confidence scores. That finding identifies a vulnerability in a design metric; mitigating it could help reduce false discoveries in binder engineering.
icml-2026-inference-time-optimization-fo.tldr: Latent optimization improves experimentally grounded protein ensembles and exposes a way to artificially inflate model confidence.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture can learn a useful compact description of the U.S. equity market. Its input consists of each trading day’s per-asset features. A jointly trained tokenizer converts that unordered collection into a fixed set of learned factor tokens, so the representation does not depend on asset ordering.

A temporal predictive model then uses masked prediction to learn daily market-state embeddings. The evaluations distinguish several kinds of market information these embeddings might contain. They are strongly associated with realized volatility, concentration of correlations, and effective factor dimensionality, but only weakly associated with market direction. Their strongest reported relationships therefore concern market variability and collective structure.

The embeddings help predict gradual recovery dynamics but do not predict sudden stress onsets. This is a substantive boundary on their demonstrated forecasting value. Even without text supervision, the learned regimes also align statistically with shifts in news topics. Together, the findings indicate that the representation captures meaningful market states while supporting some temporal predictions more effectively than others.
icml-2026-joint-embedding-predictive-lea.tldr: JEPA market embeddings capture volatility and correlation structure and help predict recoveries, but not sudden stress onsets.

paragraphs: Removing model weights does not automatically deliver proportional memory savings or faster inference. For the unstructured sparsity found in pruned language models, existing sparse matrix-vector multiplication methods can incur substantial overhead. MACKO addresses this by designing a sparse storage format and GPU computation kernel together, with memory bandwidth identified as the main bottleneck.

The format reduces storage overhead while fitting the GPU’s execution model. It supports unstructured sparsity without specialized hardware units or precomputation. This matters because the positions of surviving weights need not follow a prescribed pattern, yet the implementation still has to store and process them efficiently enough to outperform a dense representation.

At 50% sparsity, the paper reports a 1.5-fold memory reduction and a 1.2–1.5-fold speedup over the dense baseline, alongside improvements over other sparse methods. A language model pruned with Wanda achieves 1.5-fold lower memory requirements and 1.5-fold faster fp16 inference. These results support the practical value of unstructured pruning at that sparsity and narrow its efficiency gap with structured 2:4 sparsity.
icml-2026-macko-sparse-matrix-vector-mul.tldr: MACKO co-designs sparse storage and GPU execution to make 50% unstructured pruning yield practical memory and inference gains.

paragraphs: Macrocycles are ring-shaped molecules with promising selectivity and binding affinity against difficult targets. Generating them is challenging because they are scarce in public datasets and their ring structure is difficult to enforce in standard generative models. MacroGuide addresses this structural requirement by guiding pretrained molecular diffusion models during sampling.

At each denoising step, the method constructs a Vietoris-Rips complex from atomic positions and optimizes persistent homology features to encourage rings. These mathematical objects provide a way to describe ring-like structure in the developing arrangement of atoms. The guidance works both for unconditional generation and for generation conditioned on a protein pocket.

In the reported experiments, adding MacroGuide increases macrocycle generation rates from 1% to 99%. It also matches or exceeds leading performance on chemical validity, diversity, and PoseBusters checks. This combination matters because increasing ring production alone would not establish molecule quality. The findings show that topological guidance can strongly redirect pretrained generators toward macrocycles while maintaining the assessed quality properties.
icml-2026-macroguide-topological-guidanc.tldr: MacroGuide steers pretrained molecular diffusion models toward macrocycles, raising reported generation rates from 1% to 99%.

paragraphs: Some language models can notice when a steering vector is inserted into their internal activations and identify the associated concept. This paper examines the mechanism behind that behavior in open-source models. It asks whether detection reflects substantive internal anomaly processing or can be explained by a shallower heuristic.

Across diverse prompts, the studied models achieve moderate true positive rates with zero observed false positives. The capability emerges from post-training rather than pretraining. Mechanistic analysis finds that detection cannot be reduced to a single linear confound: it involves distributed computation across multiple MLP directions, including interpretable features that gate detection and carry evidence.

The authors also find that default prompting reveals only part of the available capability. Ablating refusal directions improves detection by 50%, while a trained steering vector improves it by 75%. These results support an account based on nontrivial internal anomaly detection and suggest room for improvement. The demonstrated behavior concerns awareness of injected internal changes, which is the specific operational meaning of introspection investigated here.
icml-2026-mechanisms-of-introspective-aw.tldr: Detecting injected internal concepts involves distributed anomaly-processing mechanisms, and targeted interventions improve the measured capability.

paragraphs: Complex indirect jailbreaks can exploit a model’s generation process over multiple steps, bypassing safety alignment focused on surface behavior. Reflector trains models to reflect within that process. The aim is to make checking part of the generation trajectory, so the model develops structured and increasingly autonomous reflection capabilities.

Training proceeds in two stages. First, teacher-guided generation supplies reflection examples for supervised fine-tuning, establishing the desired patterns. Second, reinforcement learning uses outcome-driven supervision together with reward-validity supervision to strengthen autonomous reflection. This links the initial demonstrations to training signals intended to support reliable behavior under attack.

The reported defense success rate exceeds 90% against complex indirect attacks, with generalization across diverse threat scenarios. Reflector also improves utility, including a 5.85% gain on GSM8K and gains on knowledge-intensive benchmarks. The authors report these benefits without significant computational overhead. The findings suggest that internalizing reflection can improve measured safety and task performance together, while the reported success rate remains an empirical result rather than a guarantee against every attack.
icml-2026-reflector-internalizing-step-w.tldr: Reflector trains step-wise self-reflection, reporting over 90% defense success against complex indirect attacks alongside utility gains.

paragraphs: Long reasoning chains can improve accuracy through exploration and self-checking, but they also increase context length and delay answers. This paper treats a language model as an operator that repeatedly improves its own work. It studies how organizing that work differently changes the tradeoff between accuracy, context length, and latency.

Parallel-Distill-Refine generates diverse drafts simultaneously, compresses them into a bounded textual workspace, and refines an answer using that workspace. The result can seed another round. Parallelism provides control over context length without equating it with all generated tokens. With one draft at a time, the method becomes Sequential Refinement, which also outperforms long-chain reasoning in reported evaluations.

The authors report PDR configurations that improve accuracy while reducing latency relative to long chains of thought. They additionally train an 8B thinking model with reinforcement learning aligned to PDR inference. On mathematics with verifiable answers, iterative approaches outperform single-pass baselines at matched sequential budgets, with PDR yielding the largest gains, including 11% on AIME 2024 and 9% on AIME 2025.
icml-2026-rethinking-thinking-tokens-llm.tldr: Parallel drafting, bounded distillation, and iterative refinement improve reported reasoning accuracy and latency tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Classical Bertrand competition predicts low prices, yet higher prices often persist in real markets. This paper investigates the gap through a repeated pricing game in which firms use no-regret learning algorithms. Its focus is how different learning guarantees shape the equilibrium outcomes that can emerge over repeated interaction.

The model has at least two firms choosing simultaneously from a finite price grid, with demand that does not increase as price rises. The lowest-priced firm receives all demand; firms tied for the lowest price split it equally. These rules define the competitive setting in which the authors compare external-regret and stronger swap-regret guarantees.

The analysis asks whether external-regret learners can approach undesirable high-price outcomes and how swap-regret guarantees influence competitive low-price behavior. Theoretical results are accompanied by experiments that support the analysis and reveal surprising behavior among swap-regret learners. The contribution is an examination of how learning rules affect pricing equilibria within this specified game, connecting algorithmic guarantees to the economic question behind the Bertrand paradox.
icml-2026-revisiting-the-bertrand-parado.tldr: The paper analyzes how external-regret and swap-regret learning shape equilibria in a repeated discrete Bertrand pricing game.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates a policy’s value using data generated under another policy. Sparse rewards make this difficult because common estimators can vary dramatically across samples. This paper introduces Reward-Shaping Control Variates, a family of unbiased estimators designed to reduce that variation without changing the expected estimate.

The method uses potential-based reward shaping to construct additional zero-mean control variates. Such terms can adjust an estimator’s fluctuations while preserving its expectation. The authors prove valid variance reduction and show that combining shaping-based terms with Q-based terms strictly enlarges the available variance-reduction subspace beyond doubly robust estimation and its minimax variant.

Experiments map performance across synthetic chains, a cancer simulator, stock-trading environments, and an ICU-sepsis benchmark. Shaping-based evaluation consistently outperforms doubly robust estimation in the tested sparse-reward settings. A hybrid estimator reports leading performance across sparse, noisy, and misspecified environments. Together, the theoretical and empirical results identify reward shaping as a source of useful evaluation information, extending its role to more stable estimates of policy value.
icml-2026-reward-shaping-control-variate.tldr: Reward-shaping control variates reduce off-policy evaluation variance while preserving unbiasedness, with strong reported results under sparse rewards.

paragraphs: A traffic-signal controller that works in a small network may struggle as intersections become more numerous and varied. Changing traffic patterns add another challenge. SLight addresses these issues through grouped multi-agent reinforcement learning, allowing intersections to share control principles while adapting their group assignments to their traffic conditions.

The framework first encodes traffic patterns with awareness of how the control policy influences them. It then learns explicit group-level principles from sequences of states and actions. A compatibility-based assignment module matches each intersection’s traffic representation to prototypes of those principles. This creates a flexible connection between local conditions and shared control behavior.

Experiments on real-world and synthetic networks report that SLight maintains performance gains as network scale increases. It outperforms rule-based, reinforcement learning, and grouping-based baselines in those evaluations. The findings support the combination of policy-aware representations and adaptive sharing: intersections can draw on common control principles without requiring a single fixed grouping to accommodate all traffic patterns and intersection differences.
icml-2026-scalable-traffic-signal-contro.tldr: SLight adaptively shares traffic-control principles across intersections and sustains reported performance gains as networks grow.

paragraphs: Generating several candidate programs is useful only if a system can identify which ones are correct. Execution-based selection can help, but obtaining informative test inputs is difficult, and random sampling can waste effort. Agentic Verifier addresses this by actively searching for inputs that distinguish candidate programs through their behavior.

The verifier interacts with a code execution environment over multiple turns. It reasons about the candidates, revises an input generator, and produces targeted counterexamples that expose disagreements. Its training pipeline combines large-scale synthesized data, rejection fine-tuning, and agentic reinforcement learning to develop this ability to generate discriminative inputs.

Across five competitive programming benchmarks, the method consistently improves over strong execution-based baselines, with reported absolute Best@k accuracy gains reaching 10–15%. Further analysis shows test-time scaling behavior, indicating that additional inference effort can support better verification in the studied setting. The results make targeted test generation a central part of choosing among candidate solutions, and the authors also identify potential uses beyond reranking.
icml-2026-scaling-agentic-verifier-for-c.tldr: Agentic Verifier learns to generate targeted tests that expose differences between candidate programs and improve solution selection.

paragraphs: A correct final answer does not establish that the mathematical reasoning behind it is valid. This paper studies how to evaluate and scale language-model proof verifiers. It first shows that conclusions based on a single benchmark can be brittle or misleading, motivating evaluation across both proof-based reasoning and final-answer problems.

The authors scale GenSelect and LLM-as-a-Judge to millions of tokens and find their combination most effective for verification and solution selection. They also examine prompt choice for the judging model. Performance is sensitive to that choice, but reinforcement learning reduces the sensitivity, making the verifier’s behavior less dependent on how the request is phrased.

A central finding qualifies the apparent progress: reinforcement learning improves proof-level metrics without improving final-answer precision. The authors interpret this mismatch as evidence that current models often reward stylistic or procedural features rather than mathematical validity. The work therefore provides both a practical combination of verification methods and a reason to assess gains using multiple complementary measures.
icml-2026-scaling-generative-verifiers-f.tldr: Combined generative verifiers perform best in the study, but improved proof metrics do not necessarily improve final-answer precision.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can make mixture-of-experts language models unstable enough for training to collapse. This paper identifies a discrepancy between the routing behavior used during inference and during training. Because routing determines expert participation, the mismatch creates inconsistency between the model behavior producing training experience and the behavior used to learn from it.

Rollout Routing Replay, or R3, records routing distributions from the inference engine and reuses them during training. The intervention directly aligns the routing behavior across the two phases. The authors report a substantial reduction in training-inference policy KL divergence, including mitigation of extreme discrepancies, without a reduction in training speed.

Experiments across various settings show stabilized reinforcement learning, prevention of collapse, and improvements over strong baselines. R3 is also compatible with most improvements to policy optimization algorithms because it addresses a different part of the training process. The findings establish routing consistency as a useful intervention point for the studied mixture-of-experts models, alongside changes to the optimization algorithm itself.
icml-2026-stabilizing-moe-reinforcement-.tldr: Replaying inference routing distributions during training stabilizes mixture-of-experts reinforcement learning without reducing reported training speed.

paragraphs: GUI grounding connects an instruction to the interface element it refers to. Attention-based methods can locate elements without task-specific fine-tuning, but their localization signals can be unreliable. Trifuse strengthens those signals by adding explicit spatial evidence from interface text and icon descriptions, reducing reliance on large annotated GUI datasets.

The framework combines model attention, text cues obtained through optical character recognition, and semantic captions for icons. Its Consensus-SinglePeak fusion strategy encourages agreement among these sources while preserving sharp localization peaks. This addresses two linked needs: corroborating the likely target and retaining a precise location instead of spreading support broadly across the screen.

Evaluations on four grounding benchmarks report strong performance without task-specific fine-tuning. Ablation studies also show that adding OCR and caption information consistently improves attention-based grounding across different model backbones. These findings support complementary spatial anchors as a general way to strengthen attention-based localization, with the reported benefits extending beyond a single underlying model architecture.
icml-2026-trifuse-enhancing-attention-ba.tldr: Trifuse combines attention, recognized text, and icon captions to improve GUI grounding without task-specific fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Forecasting cancer care trajectories requires handling patient histories that are sparse, multimodal, and spread across time. TwinWeaver converts those longitudinal histories into text so a language model can support both event prediction and forecasting. The authors use this open-source framework to build Genie Digital Twin from 93,054 patients spanning 20 cancer types.

In benchmark forecasting, the model achieves a median Mean Absolute Scaled Error of 0.87, compared with 0.97 for the strongest time-series baseline. For risk stratification across survival, progression, and therapy switching, its average concordance index is 0.703 versus 0.662 for the best baseline. These results show improvements across two distinct types of longitudinal prediction.

On out-of-distribution clinical trials, the model matches trained baselines without task-specific training and surpasses them after fine-tuning. Reported fine-tuned results include median forecasting errors of 0.75–0.88 and an average event-prediction concordance index of 0.672 versus 0.648. TwinWeaver also supports an interpretable clinical reasoning extension, broadening the framework beyond its core predictive outputs.
icml-2026-twinweaver-an-llm-based-founda.tldr: TwinWeaver turns longitudinal cancer histories into text for language-model forecasting and event prediction, improving reported benchmark performance.

paragraphs: When reinforcement learning improves a vision-language model equipped with crop-and-zoom tools, the gain could have several sources. The model might become better at using tools, improve its underlying visual reasoning, or simply make fewer mistakes caused by tool access. This paper introduces MED, a framework for separating those explanations.

MED measures changes in intrinsic capability separately from tool-induced effects, then divides the latter into gains and harms. It also investigates mechanisms behind their evolution. The authors apply this analysis across training checkpoints for two vision-language models with different prior tool capabilities and evaluate them on six benchmarks.

The observed improvements are dominated by intrinsic learning. Tool-use training primarily reduces harm, including errors introduced by calls and interference from tool schemas, while producing limited progress in using tools to correct failures of the underlying model. The findings therefore qualify what overall accuracy gains demonstrate: in these experiments, learning to avoid tool-related disruption accounts for more of the tool-specific progress than learning to rescue otherwise unsuccessful reasoning.
icml-2026-what-does-vision-tool-use-rein.tldr: MED finds that studied vision tool-use RL gains mainly reflect intrinsic learning and reduced tool-induced harm, with limited tool-based correction.
